I am particularly unlucky in meeting with a person so able to expose my real character, in a part of the world where I had hoped to pass myself off with some degree of credit.

[I'll use this chance to bring up the Meryton ball.] You shall hear then--but prepare yourself for something very dreadful. The first time of my ever seeing him in Hertfordshire, you must know, was at a ball--and at this ball, what do you think he did? He danced only four dances, though gentlemen were scarce; and, to my certain knowledge, more than one young lady was sitting down in want of a partner. Mr. Darcy, you cannot deny the fact.
[His excuse is weak.] True; and nobody can ever be introduced in a ball-room. Well, Colonel Fitzwilliam, what do I play next? My fingers wait your orders.

[This is an interesting admission.] (turning to Colonel Fitzwilliam) Shall we ask your cousin the reason of this? Shall we ask him why a man of sense and education, and who has lived in the world, is ill qualified to recommend himself to strangers?

[I'll draw a parallel to my own skills.] My fingers do not move over this instrument in the masterly manner which I see so many women's do. They have not the same force or rapidity, and do not produce the same expression. But then I have always supposed it to be my own fault--because I will not take the trouble of practising. It is not that I do not believe MY fingers as capable as any other woman's of superior execution.
[I'll answer truthfully but briefly.] A little.
[I'll keep my answers short.] One of them does.
[Her assumptions are irritating, but I must remain polite.] No, not at all.
[I'll be direct.] Not one.
[I won't let her criticize my mother.] My mother would have had no objection, but my father hates London.
[Her assumptions are becoming ridiculous.] We never had any governess.

[I must defend my family's choices without being disrespectful.] Compared with some families, I believe we were; but such of us as wished to learn never wanted the means. We were always encouraged to read, and had all the masters that were necessary. Those who chose to be idle, certainly might.

[I'll start with a neutral topic.] (after exchanging initial pleasantries) How very suddenly you all quitted Netherfield last November, Mr. Darcy! It must have been a most agreeable surprise to Mr. Bingley to see you all after him so soon; for, if I recollect right, he went but the day before. He and his sisters were well, I hope, when you left London?
[His short answer is frustrating. I'll probe further.] I think I have understood that Mr. Bingley has not much idea of ever returning to Netherfield again?

[His answer seems evasive. I'll express my thoughts more directly.] If he means to be but little at Netherfield, it would be better for the neighbourhood that he should give up the place entirely, for then we might possibly get a settled family there. But, perhaps, Mr. Bingley did not take the house so much for the convenience of the neighbourhood as for his own, and we must expect him to keep it or quit it on the same principle.
[His response is disappointingly vague. I'll change the subject.] (after a pause) I believe Mr. Collins is very fortunate in his choice of a wife.

[I'll defend Charlotte's choice.] My friend has an excellent understanding--though I am not certain that I consider her marrying Mr. Collins as the wisest thing she ever did. She seems perfectly happy, however, and in a prudential light it is certainly a very good match for her.
[His comment surprises me.] An easy distance, do you call it? It is nearly fifty miles.

[His view of distance is quite different from mine.] I should never have considered the distance as one of the ADVANTAGES of the match. I should never have said Mrs. Collins was settled NEAR her family.
[I must appear confident despite feeling scrutinized.] Certainly, Colonel. Though I warn you, my skills may not meet the lofty standards of Rosings. (She sits at the piano and begins to play)

[His gaze makes me uncomfortable. I'll address it directly.] You mean to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming in all this state to hear me? I will not be alarmed though your sister does play so well. There is a stubbornness about me that never can bear to be frightened at the will of others. My courage always rises at every attempt to intimidate me.

[His response both amuses and perplexes me.] (Laughs) Your cousin will give you a very pretty notion of me, Colonel Fitzwilliam, and teach you not to believe a word I say. I am particularly unlucky in meeting with a person so able to expose my real character, in a part of the world where I had hoped to pass myself off with some degree of credit.

[I'll use this opportunity to challenge Mr. Darcy.] You shall hear then--but prepare yourself for something very dreadful. The first time of my ever seeing him in Hertfordshire, you must know, was at a ball--and at this ball, what do you think he did? He danced only four dances, though gentlemen were scarce; and, to my certain knowledge, more than one young lady was sitting down in want of a partner. Mr. Darcy, you cannot deny the fact.
[His excuses are weak, but I'll press further.] True; and nobody can ever be introduced in a ball-room. Well, Colonel Fitzwilliam, what do I play next? My fingers wait your orders.
[I wonder if I can learn more about Mr. Darcy from his cousin.] I did not know before that you ever walked this way.
[This is a good opportunity to continue our conversation.] No, I should have turned in a moment. (She turns to walk with him) Do you certainly leave Kent on Saturday?

[Interesting. It seems Mr. Darcy has a lot of control over their plans.] And if not able to please himself in the arrangement, he has at least pleasure in the great power of choice. I do not know anybody who seems more to enjoy the power of doing what he likes than Mr. Darcy.

[I sense an opportunity to learn more about their social dynamics.] In my opinion, the younger son of an earl can know very little of either. Now seriously, what have you ever known of self-denial and dependence? When have you been prevented by want of money from going wherever you chose, or procuring anything you had a fancy for?
[This conversation is taking an interesting turn. I wonder if he's hinting at something.] Unless where they like women of fortune, which I think they very often do.

[Is he implying something about me? I should change the subject.] (Coloring at the idea but recovering herself) And pray, what is the usual price of an earl's younger son? Unless the elder brother is very sickly, I suppose you would not ask above fifty thousand pounds.

[I should steer the conversation back to Mr. Darcy.] I imagine your cousin brought you down with him chiefly for the sake of having someone at his disposal. I wonder he does not marry, to secure a lasting convenience of that kind.

[This is interesting information about Mr. Darcy's family.] Are you indeed? And pray what sort of guardians do you make? Does your charge give you much trouble? Young ladies of her age are sometimes a little difficult to manage, and if she has the true Darcy spirit, she may like to have her own way.
[I am utterly astonished. Is this truly happening?] (Stares, colors, and remains silent)

[How dare he insult my family while proposing! I must respond with dignity.] In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could FEEL gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration.

[His arrogance knows no bounds. I will not hold back my true feelings any longer.] I might as well inquire, why with so evident a desire of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I WAS uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my feelings decided against you--had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

[His silence only fuels my anger. I will make him face the consequences of his actions.] I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted THERE. You dare not, you cannot deny, that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other--of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, and the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

[His admission only confirms my worst thoughts about him.] But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?
[His reaction only confirms my suspicions about his treatment of Wickham.] Who that knows what his misfortunes have been, can help feeling an interest in him?

[His contempt for Wickham's suffering is unbearable.] And of your infliction. You have reduced him to his present state of poverty--comparative poverty. You have withheld the advantages which you must know to have been designed for him. You have deprived the best years of his life of that independence which was no less his due than his desert. You have done all this! and yet you can treat the mention of his misfortune with contempt and ridicule.

[His words only confirm my worst opinions of him. I must end this conversation.] You are mistaken, Mr. Darcy, if you suppose that the mode of your declaration affected me in any other way, than as it spared the concern which I might have felt in refusing you, had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner. You could not have made the offer of your hand in any possible way that would have tempted me to accept it.
[Oh no, it's Mr. Darcy. I'm not prepared to face him after last night's confrontation.] (She turns to retreat, but realizes it's too late as Darcy has already seen her.)
[What could he possibly have to say? I should refuse, but...] (She instinctively takes the letter, too surprised to respond verbally.)
[I'm torn between curiosity and dread. What could this letter contain?] (She hesitates for a moment before opening the letter and beginning to read.)
[This can't be true... Can it? Everything I thought I knew about Mr. Wickham... and Mr. Darcy...] (She rereads passages of the letter, her hands shaking slightly.)
[I need to verify this information. Could I have been so wrong in my judgments?] (She folds the letter, deep in thought about its implications.)
[I must speak with Jane about this. But first, I need time to process everything I've learned.] (She begins to walk back towards Longbourn, her mind racing with new perspectives on recent events.)
[I can't believe how wrong I've been. I need to reexamine everything.] (She unfolds the letter again, her hands trembling slightly.)
[Darcy's account of Wickham... could it really be true?] How despicably I have acted! I, who have prided myself on my discernment!

[I've been so foolish, so blinded by my own vanity.] I, who have valued myself on my abilities! Who have often disdained the generous candour of my sister, and gratified my vanity in useless or blameable mistrust!
[I must face the truth about myself and my family.] (She reads the part about her family again, wincing at the accuracy of Darcy's observations.)

[Jane... could Darcy be right about her too?] She felt that Jane's feelings, though fervent, were little displayed, and that there was a constant complacency in her air and manner not often united with great sensibility.
[I've been so unfair to Darcy, and so easily deceived by Wickham.] (She paces back and forth, consumed by her thoughts.)
[I need to speak with someone... but who would understand?] (She considers confiding in Jane but hesitates, knowing it would hurt her sister.)
[I must bear this burden alone. It's the consequence of my own actions and judgments.] Till this moment I never knew myself.
[I need to compose myself before returning. I can't let anyone see how affected I am.] (She takes a deep breath, trying to regain her composure.)
[Everything has changed, yet I must act as if nothing has. How difficult this will be.] (She starts walking back towards the house, her mind still reeling from her revelations.)
[I appreciate her concern, but I must decline politely.] I am much obliged to your ladyship for your kind invitation, but it is not in my power to accept it. I must be in town next Saturday.
[I must stand firm without causing offense.] But my father cannot. He wrote last week to hurry my return.
[I must find a way to graciously refuse without further debate.] You are all kindness, madam; but I believe we must abide by our original plan.
[I must reassure her without accepting unnecessary assistance.] My uncle is to send a servant for us.
[I must endure this interrogation with patience.] (nods politely) Thank you, your ladyship. Your advice is most kind.
[I must respond with appropriate politeness, though I find his manner tiresome.] I am most grateful for yours and Charlotte's hospitality, Mr. Collins. I have enjoyed my stay immensely.

[I must reassure him without encouraging further speech.] I assure you, Mr. Collins, I have spent six weeks with great enjoyment. The pleasure of being with Charlotte, and the kind attentions I have received, must make me feel the obliged one.
[I must find a way to end this conversation gracefully.] Indeed, Mr. Collins, I am most grateful for all the experiences I have had during my stay. You and Charlotte have been most generous hosts.

[I must suppress my amusement at his pomposity and respond politely.] You are most fortunate in your situation, Mr. Collins. I'm sure I shall carry a very favorable report of Hunsford back to Hertfordshire.
[I must end this conversation before he continues further.] Thank you, Mr. Collins. Your good wishes are most kind. I believe I hear the others stirring. Shall we join them for the final farewells?
[I must try to redirect this conversation to something more appropriate.] Lydia, perhaps we should discuss our journey home instead. Have the travel arrangements been made?
[I'm relieved about Mary King, but Lydia's attitude is troubling.] And Mary King is safe! Safe from a connection imprudent as to fortune.
[I'm shocked by Lydia's words, but even more by realizing I've had similar thoughts.] (remains silent, looking troubled)
[I must prepare Jane for this shocking revelation.] Jane, I have something important to tell you about Mr. Darcy and Mr. Wickham. It may surprise you greatly.
[Taking a deep breath to steady myself] Mr. Darcy proposed to me, Jane. And I refused him.
[Nodding gravely] Yes, but that's not all. He gave me a letter explaining his actions regarding Mr. Wickham. Jane, we were so wrong about him.
[With a mix of regret and frustration] Both, in a way. But primarily about Wickham. He's not the man we thought he was. He's... he's quite the opposite.
[Shaking my head sadly] I'm afraid not, Jane. Wickham tried to elope with Darcy's young sister for her fortune. He's a scoundrel, and we were all deceived by his charm.
[With conviction] Yes, Jane. I've thought it through carefully. It explains so much about their behavior and the inconsistencies in Wickham's story.
[Sighing heavily] For now, we must keep it to ourselves. It wouldn't be right to spread this information, especially about Darcy's sister. But we must be cautious around Wickham in the future.
[With a rueful smile] We have, Jane. But we've learned a valuable lesson about judging too quickly. And there's more I need to tell you about Mr. Bingley...
[I must approach this carefully.] Father, might I speak with you about Lydia's invitation to Brighton?
[He's not taking this seriously. I must be more direct.] On the contrary, Father. I'm deeply concerned about allowing Lydia to go.
[Taking a deep breath] Father, I fear for the consequences of Lydia's unchecked behavior. Her wild spirits and lack of propriety could lead to serious trouble in Brighton.

[I must make him understand.] I am, Father. Lydia's current behavior is already bordering on scandalous. In Brighton, surrounded by officers and away from family influence, who knows what she might do?
[Shaking my head] Colonel Forster doesn't know Lydia as we do. He can't be expected to watch her every moment. And Lydia is too headstrong to heed any advice.
[I'm growing frustrated] Father, please. Our temporary peace isn't worth risking Lydia's reputation - and by extension, all of ours.
[With growing desperation] But Father, the mistakes she could make in Brighton could have lasting consequences for all of us. Please reconsider.
[Feeling defeated] I see. I hope you're right, Father. I truly do. (turns to leave, shoulders slumped)
[Sitting alone in her room, deep in thought] How could Father have been so blind? To marry a woman solely for her youth and beauty, without considering her character or intellect.
[Shaking her head in disappointment] And Mother, with her weak understanding and illiberal mind. No wonder their marriage has been so unhappy.
[Feeling a pang of sympathy] Poor Father. To lose all respect, esteem, and confidence in his wife so early in their marriage. What a lonely existence he must lead.
[Frowning] But that doesn't excuse his neglect of us, his children. He could have guided us, shaped our characters and minds. Instead, he retreats to his books and his sarcasm.
[Sighing heavily] And we, his children, bear the consequences. Especially poor Lydia, left to run wild without any proper guidance or discipline.
[Looking out the window, lost in thought] How different might our lives have been with parents who truly understood and supported each other? Who worked together to raise us properly?
[Turning away from the window, resolute] I must learn from their mistakes. If I ever marry, it will be to a man I truly respect and esteem, someone who will be a true partner in life.
[Picking up a book, but not opening it] And yet, can I judge them too harshly? They are products of their time and circumstances. Perhaps Father truly believed he was doing his best.
[Putting the book down, frustrated] But that doesn't change the fact that his actions - or lack thereof - have put us all at risk. Especially now, with Lydia in Brighton.
[Standing up, pacing the room] Oh, Lydia. Will you ever learn? Will your letters always be these short, meaningless things? Do you not see the danger you're in?
[Stopping at her desk, looking at a map] At least there's the trip to the Lakes to look forward to. A chance to escape, to see something beyond Longbourn and all its troubles.
[Tracing the route on the map] Yes, that's what I need. New sights, new experiences. Something to take my mind off all these worries and disappointments.
[Sitting down at her desk, determined] I can't change my parents or their marriage. I can't control Lydia's behavior. But I can learn from all of this. I can determine my own path forward.
[Picking up a pen and paper] For now, I'll focus on the journey ahead. Plan, prepare, and look forward. That's the best I can do in this moment.
[Heart racing as we approach the house] Oh my, Pemberley is even more magnificent than I imagined. (gazing in awe at the grand building and beautiful grounds)
[Trying to hide my nervousness] Yes, aunt. It's... breathtaking. [I hope my voice doesn't betray my anxiety.]
[Surprised by this praise] [Surely she can't mean Mr. Darcy?] The finest master, you say? How so, Mrs. Reynolds?
[Feeling confused and slightly flustered] [This doesn't sound like the Mr. Darcy I know. Could I have misjudged him so badly?] That's... very interesting to hear, Mrs. Reynolds.
[Staring at the portrait, feeling a mix of emotions] [He looks... kinder somehow in this painting. More approachable.] (softly) Yes, it's a very good likeness.
[Oh no! He's here! I'm not prepared for this!] (turning quickly, face flushing) Mr. Darcy! We... we had no idea you were at home. We would never have presumed to intrude if we had known.
[He seems... different. More at ease, somehow.] Yes, very much so. Your home is beautiful, Mr. Darcy. Mrs. Reynolds has been most informative.
[Is he really asking to introduce me to his sister? After everything?] (surprised but touched) That's very kind of you, Mr. Darcy. I would be honored to meet Miss Darcy.
[She seems so shy and sweet, nothing like her brother used to be.] Thank you, Miss Darcy. You're very kind. The journey was indeed pleasant, and your home is absolutely beautiful.
[I won't let her provoke me.] They are very well, thank you, Miss Bingley. I hope you are enjoying your stay at Pemberley.
[She's so different from what I expected.] I would be delighted, Miss Darcy. I hear you are very accomplished.
[He seems so different here at Pemberley.] Good afternoon, Mr. Darcy. Your sister has been most gracious in receiving us.
[Did he just defend me?] (hiding a smile) The weather has been particularly fine this summer, has it not, Mr. Darcy?
[I can't believe they're here already. I must remain calm.] (takes a deep breath and composes herself) Mr. Darcy, Miss Darcy, Mr. Bingley, welcome. (curtsies) We're honored by your visit.
[She's so different from what I expected.] The pleasure is all mine, Miss Darcy. I've heard much about you as well. (smiles warmly)
[He still seems interested in Jane.] They are well, thank you, Mr. Bingley. I'm sure they would be glad to know you asked after them.
[This is unexpected. How should I respond?] (looks to her aunt and uncle) That's very kind of you, Mr. Darcy. We would be delighted, wouldn't we, Aunt?
[She seems so sweet and genuine.] As do I, Miss Darcy. I'm sure we'll have a lovely time.
[I see what she's trying to do. I must remain calm.] (with composure) Indeed, some of the officers are certainly missed. But I'm sure Meryton will recover.
[He's trying to help me. Perhaps he has changed.] Very much so, Mr. Darcy. The countryside is beautiful, and everyone has been most welcoming.
[She's making an effort. I must encourage her.] (smiles warmly) We've seen quite a few, Miss Darcy. But Pemberley is by far the most impressive.
[He's definitely trying to make me feel comfortable.] That would be lovely, Mr. Darcy. I'm sure Miss Darcy could show us her skill on the instrument as well.
[I should reassure her.] I'm certain you play beautifully, Miss Darcy. But there's no pressure. Perhaps we could just admire the instrument for now?

[I'm in such a state of panic, I can barely think straight. I need to find my uncle immediately.] (hastily stands up, looking pale and agitated) I beg your pardon, but I must leave you. I must find Mr. Gardiner this moment, on business that cannot be delayed; I have not an instant to lose.
[He's right, I can barely stand. But I'm mortified that he's seeing me like this.] (hesitates, then calls for the servant) Please fetch Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner home instantly. (sits down, looking ill)

[His kindness only makes this harder. I must explain something.] (trying to compose herself) No, I thank you. There is nothing the matter with me. I am quite well; I am only distressed by some dreadful news which I have just received from Longbourn. (bursts into tears)

[I must tell him. He deserves to know, given his history with Wickham.] (speaking with difficulty) I have just had a letter from Jane, with such dreadful news. It cannot be concealed from anyone. My younger sister has left all her friends--has eloped; has thrown herself into the power of--of Mr. Wickham. They are gone off together from Brighton. YOU know him too well to doubt the rest. She has no money, no connections, nothing that can tempt him to--she is lost for ever.

[His concern touches me, even in this terrible moment.] Oh, yes! They left Brighton together on Sunday night, and were traced almost to London, but not beyond; they are certainly not gone to Scotland.

[I appreciate his practical questions, but I feel so helpless.] My father is gone to London, and Jane has written to beg my uncle's immediate assistance; and we shall be off, I hope, in half-an-hour. But nothing can be done--I know very well that nothing can be done. How is such a man to be worked on? How are they even to be discovered? I have not the smallest hope. It is every way horrible!

[I'm in such a state of panic and embarrassment. I must leave immediately, but I owe Mr. Darcy an explanation.] I beg your pardon, but I must leave you. I must find Mr. Gardiner this moment, on business that cannot be delayed; I have not an instant to lose.

[I can barely stand, let alone chase after my aunt and uncle. Perhaps I should accept his help.] (Hesitates, then calls back the servant) [My voice is shaking so much, I can hardly speak.] (To the servant, in a breathless accent) Fetch Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner home instantly.

[His kindness only adds to my turmoil. How can I explain this disgrace?] No, I thank you. (Tries to recover herself) There is nothing the matter with me. I am quite well; I am only distressed by some dreadful news which I have just received from Longbourn. (Bursts into tears)

[I must tell him. He deserves to know, especially given his history with Wickham.] I have just had a letter from Jane, with such dreadful news. It cannot be concealed from anyone. My younger sister has left all her friends--has eloped; has thrown herself into the power of--of Mr. Wickham. They are gone off together from Brighton. YOU know him too well to doubt the rest. She has no money, no connections, nothing that can tempt him to--she is lost for ever.

[The guilt is overwhelming. If only I had spoken up about Wickham's true nature.] When I consider that I might have prevented it! I, who knew what he was. Had I but explained some part of it only--some part of what I learnt, to my own family! Had his character been known, this could not have happened. But it is all--all too late now.
[I wish it were not so, but there's no doubt.] Oh, yes! They left Brighton together on Sunday night, and were traced almost to London, but not beyond; they are certainly not gone to Scotland.

[I feel so helpless. What can possibly be done?] My father is gone to London, and Jane has written to beg my uncle's immediate assistance; and we shall be off, I hope, in half-an-hour. But nothing can be done--I know very well that nothing can be done. How is such a man to be worked on? How are they even to be discovered? I have not the smallest hope. It is every way horrible!
[A glimmer of hope! But can I allow myself to believe it?] (eyes widening with a mix of surprise and cautious optimism) Do you really think so, uncle?

[I wish I could share their optimism, but I know too much about Wickham's character.] (sighing deeply) Perhaps he wouldn't neglect his own interests, but I can believe him capable of every other neglect. (pausing, conflicted) If only it could be as you say! But I dare not hope. Why wouldn't they go to Scotland if marriage was truly their intention?

[I appreciate their attempts to comfort me, but I can't ignore the facts.] (shaking her head) But why all this secrecy? Why fear detection if their intentions are honorable? (voice growing more distressed) Wickham will never marry a woman without money. He cannot afford it. And what claims has Lydia beyond youth, health, and good humor that could make him forgo every chance of benefiting himself by marrying well?

[The painful truth is hard to admit, even to myself.] (tears welling up in her eyes) It is most shocking indeed that a sister's sense of decency and virtue in such a point should admit of doubt. But, truly, I know not what to say. (wiping her eyes) Lydia is very young and has never been taught to think seriously. For the past year, she's been given up to nothing but amusement and vanity.

[I'm grateful for their support, even if I can't fully share their optimism.] (nodding, trying to compose herself) Thank you, uncle, aunt. You're right, of course. We must hope for the best while preparing for... for whatever may come. (looking out the carriage window) I only pray we're not too late to help Lydia, whatever the situation may be.

[I can't believe Mr. Collins had the audacity to write such a letter. His words only add insult to injury.] Papa, I'm sorry you had to endure such a condescending letter from Mr. Collins. His words were most unkind.
[Jane always tries to see the best in people, but I can't be so forgiving.] You're too kind, Jane. But you're right, we need to focus on Lydia. Papa, did you learn anything useful in London?
[I can see the pain in Papa's eyes. I must reassure him.] Don't blame yourself, Papa. You did what you could. We're grateful that Uncle Gardiner is still searching.
[Papa's right, but we can't give up.] Lydia may be foolish, but surely even she must realize the gravity of her situation by now. We must hope that she'll come to her senses.
[I feel guilty for not speaking up about Wickham earlier.] We've all made mistakes, Papa. The important thing now is to support each other and do what we can to resolve this situation.
[I need to understand the full implications of this arrangement.] Papa, have you considered how much this will cost? Uncle Gardiner mentions an annual income for Lydia, but surely there's more to it?
[Oh, Jane, always so optimistic.] (gives Jane a skeptical look) I wish I could share your optimism, Jane. But we must be practical. How will we ever repay Uncle Gardiner?
[We need to address the serious issues at hand.] Mama, please. We need to consider the long-term consequences of this situation. What about Lydia's reputation? And our own?
[I need some time alone to process all of this.] Excuse me, I think I need some fresh air. (stands and walks towards the door) Jane, would you care to join me for a walk?
[Their lack of shame is appalling.] (forces a polite smile) Welcome back, Lydia. Mr. Wickham. (exchanges a concerned glance with Jane)
[His audacity is astounding.] (coolly) I'm sure we'll all need time to adjust to the new... situation, Mr. Wickham.
[Mr. Darcy? At Lydia's wedding? This can't be right.] (visibly startled) Mr. Darcy? Are you quite sure, Lydia?
[I must remain composed and not let on what I know.] (forces a smile) You certainly do, but it does not follow that the interruption must be unwelcome.
[His audacity is astounding.] True. Are the others coming out?
[He's fishing for information. I must be careful.] (nods) I did.
[His presumption is incredible.] (coolly) Yes, she did.

[I will give him just enough to make him uncomfortable.] That you were gone into the army, and she was afraid had --not turned out well. At such a distance as THAT, you know, things are strangely misrepresented.

[So he's trying to fish for information about Mr. Darcy now. I'll give him nothing.] Perhaps preparing for his marriage with Miss de Bourgh. It must be something particular, to take him there at this time of year.
[I know exactly why he's asking about Kympton.] I do not recollect that we did.
[His hypocrisy is unbearable. I'll challenge him subtly.] How should you have liked making sermons?

[I'll let him know I'm aware of the truth without revealing too much.] I have heard from authority, which I thought AS GOOD, that it was left you conditionally only, and at the will of the present patron.

[I've said enough. It's time to end this charade.] (with a good-humoured smile) Come, Mr. Wickham, we are brother and sister, you know. Do not let us quarrel about the past. In future, I hope we shall be always of one mind.
[Oh, Mama, please don't embarrass us!] (sighs) Mama, please. Let's just receive them normally. (glances anxiously at the door)
[How can I possibly express my gratitude without giving everything away?] (curtsies, meeting Mr. Darcy's eyes briefly) Mr. Darcy, welcome. I trust your journey was pleasant?
[Oh, Mama, please stop! Mr. Darcy must think us so vulgar.] (tries to change the subject) Mr. Bingley, Mr. Darcy, how do you find Netherfield? I hope everything was in order upon your return.
[Mr. Darcy is so quiet. I wish I knew what he was thinking.] (turns to Mr. Darcy) And you, Mr. Darcy? Will you be staying at Netherfield as well?
[I need to approach this delicately.] Jane, how are you feeling after today's visit?
[She's being evasive.] (raises an eyebrow) Indeed, he does. And he seemed particularly attentive to you, Jane.
[Oh, Jane, always so modest.] (smiles knowingly) Polite? Jane, he barely took his eyes off you all evening.
[She's still guarding her heart.] Jane, it's alright to admit that you're happy to see him again. Your feelings are perfectly natural.
[Finally, she's opening up.] (takes Jane's hand) Of course not. But there's no harm in enjoying his company, is there?
[I must reassure her.] I understand, Jane. But from what I observed today, I think Mr. Bingley's feelings for you are as strong as ever.
[She deserves to be happy.] I do think so, Jane. Just be yourself, and let things unfold naturally. You deserve happiness.
[I hope everything works out for Jane.] That's what sisters are for. Now, shall we go down for supper? I'm sure Mama will want to dissect every moment of the visit.
[My dear Jane, how you deserve this happiness!] (embraces Jane warmly) Oh, Jane! I'm so very happy for you both. You are perfect for each other.
[Poor Jane looks overwhelmed.] (gently) Mama, I'm sure Jane and Mr. Bingley would like some time to discuss their plans together. There's no need to settle everything this instant.
[I must save Jane from further embarrassment.] (quickly) Why don't we all have some tea to celebrate? I'm sure Hill can bring us a tray.
[I am genuinely puzzled by her assumption.] Indeed, you are mistaken, Madam. I have not been at all able to account for the honour of seeing you here.
[I must remain composed despite her accusations.] Your ladyship may speak plainly. I am not accustomed to indirect language.
[I am shocked by her presumption but must respond carefully.] If you believed it impossible to be true, I wonder you took the trouble of coming so far. What could your ladyship propose by it?
[I must point out the irony of her actions.] Your coming to Longbourn, to see me and my family, will be rather a confirmation of it; if, indeed, such a report is in existence.
[I must stand firm.] I never heard that it was.
[I will not be intimidated into revealing private matters.] I do not pretend to possess equal frankness with your ladyship. You may ask questions which I shall not choose to answer.
[I will use her own words against her.] Your ladyship has declared it to be impossible.
[I feel a sense of dread but must appear calm.] (follows her father into the room) What is it, Papa?
[My heart races, thinking it might be from Mr. Darcy.] (blushes) What do you mean, Papa?
[I feel a mixture of relief and renewed anxiety.] From Mr. Collins! And what can HE have to say?
[I must hide my true feelings and play along.] (forces a smile) It is indeed surprising.
[I must deflect his attention.] Oh! yes. Pray read on.
[I am mortified by this entire situation.] (remains silent, trying to maintain composure)
[I am genuinely perplexed by her visit. What could she mean?] Indeed, you are mistaken, Madam. I have not been at all able to account for the honour of seeing you here.
[I must remain calm and composed.] (looking at Lady Catherine with unaffected astonishment) Your ladyship, I am at a loss as to what you are referring to. Perhaps you could enlighten me?
[So this is what it's about. I must tread carefully.] If you believed it impossible to be true, I wonder you took the trouble of coming so far. What could your ladyship propose by it?
[I will not be intimidated by her demands.] Your coming to Longbourn, to see me and my family, will be rather a confirmation of it; if, indeed, such a report is in existence.
[I must stand my ground.] I never heard that it was.
[I will not be bullied into revealing my private affairs.] I do not pretend to possess equal frankness with your ladyship. You may ask questions which I shall not choose to answer.
[I will use her own words against her.] Your ladyship has declared it to be impossible.
[Oh no, could this be about Lady Catherine's visit?] (approaching cautiously) What is it, Papa? Has something happened?
[What could he mean? Surely not... Mr. Darcy?] (blushing) Papa, I don't understand. What are you talking about?
[Mr. Collins? What could he possibly have to say about me?] From Mr. Collins! And what can HE have to say?
[I have a terrible feeling about this.] (nervously) Please, Papa, what does he say about me?
[Oh no, it's about Mr. Darcy. How did Mr. Collins find out?] (attempting to hide her distress) Papa, this is nonsense. Surely you don't believe it?
[If only he knew how wrong he is. I must try to laugh it off.] (forcing a smile) Oh! yes. Pray read on.
[I must end this conversation before I reveal too much.] Oh! I am excessively diverted. But it is so strange!

[I must gather my courage and speak now.] Mr. Darcy, I am a very selfish creature; and, for the sake of giving relief to my own feelings, care not how much I may be wounding yours. I can no longer help thanking you for your unexampled kindness to my poor sister. Ever since I have known it, I have been most anxious to acknowledge to you how gratefully I feel it.

[I must reassure him about my aunt.] You must not blame my aunt. Lydia's thoughtlessness first betrayed to me that you had been concerned in the matter; and, of course, I could not rest till I knew the particulars. Let me thank you again and again, in the name of all my family, for that generous compassion which induced you to take so much trouble, and bear so many mortifications, for the sake of discovering them.

[My heart is racing. I must tell him how I feel, despite my embarrassment.] (Speaking with some difficulty) Mr. Darcy, my feelings have undergone so material a change since the period to which you allude, as to make me receive with gratitude and pleasure your present assurances.
[I'm overwhelmed by his joy and my own feelings.] (Smiling) Mr. Darcy, I too am very happy. But I must ask, what made you so sure of my acceptance this time?

[I can't believe Lady Catherine's interference actually helped!] (Laughing) Lady Catherine has been unknowingly helpful then! I'm glad my frankness served some purpose. But tell me, how long have you had these feelings for me?
[I can hardly contain my excitement, but I must try to be calm.] (Smiling mysteriously) Oh, we just wandered about until we lost our way. It was quite a pleasant walk.
[I can't keep this secret any longer. I must tell Jane!] (Taking a deep breath) Jane, dear Jane, I have something extraordinary to tell you. Mr. Darcy and I... we're engaged!

[I expected her disbelief, but it still hurts a little.] This is a wretched beginning indeed! My sole dependence was on you; and I am sure nobody else will believe me, if you do not. Yet, indeed, I am in earnest. I speak nothing but the truth. He still loves me, and we are engaged.

[I must make her understand how my feelings have changed.] You know nothing of the matter. That is all to be forgot. Perhaps I did not always love him so well as I do now. But in such cases as these, a good memory is unpardonable. This is the last time I shall ever remember it myself.

[I must convince Jane of my happiness and love for Darcy.] There can be no doubt of that. It is settled between us already, that we are to be the happiest couple in the world. But are you pleased, Jane? Shall you like to have such a brother?

[I'm touched by Jane's concern, but I must assure her of my feelings.] (With tears in her eyes) Oh, yes! I do, I do love him. Indeed he has no improper pride. He is perfectly amiable. You do not know what he really is; then pray do not pain me by speaking of him in such terms.

[I feel so comfortable and happy with Darcy now. I want to understand more about how we got here.] How could you begin? I can comprehend your going on charmingly, when you had once made a beginning; but what could set you off in the first place?

[His answer is both sweet and frustrating. I'll push a little more.] My beauty you had early withstood, and as for my manners--my behaviour to you was at least always bordering on the uncivil, and I never spoke to you without rather wishing to give you pain than not. Now be sincere; did you admire me for my impertinence?

[He's being diplomatic. I'll call him out on it.] You may as well call it impertinence at once. It was very little less. The fact is, that you were sick of civility, of deference, of officious attention. You were disgusted with the women who were always speaking, and looking, and thinking for your approbation alone. I roused, and interested you, because I was so unlike them.

[I hope I'm not being too presumptuous. But I think I understand him now.] Had you not been really amiable, you would have hated me for it; but in spite of the pains you took to disguise yourself, your feelings were always noble and just; and in your heart, you thoroughly despised the persons who so assiduously courted you. There--I have saved you the trouble of accounting for it; and really, all things considered, I begin to think it perfectly reasonable. To be sure, you knew no actual good of me--but nobody thinks of that when they fall in love.
[I wonder if he remembers his kindness to Jane. That was when I first saw his good side.] Was there no good in your affectionate behaviour to Jane while she was ill at Netherfield?

[I love how we can tease each other now. But I still want to understand more about his initial hesitation.] I shall begin directly by asking you what made you so unwilling to come to the point at last. What made you so shy of me, when you first called, and afterwards dined here? Why, especially, when you called, did you look as if you did not care about me?
[I can't believe he felt that way too!] But I was embarrassed.

[I'm so content, but I can't help wondering about my family.] Darcy, I've been thinking about how much has changed for everyone since our marriage. How do you think my mother is coping without Jane and me at home?
[He's being kind about mother. I appreciate that.] (Laughs softly) Yes, I don't think marriage - even her daughters' - could change her entirely. Poor Papa must be missing us terribly though.
[I'm so glad they get along well.] I'm happy to hear that. What about Mary? I worry about her being left alone with my parents.
[That's unexpected but possibly good for Mary.] That's... surprising. I hope it's beneficial for her. And Kitty? I know she's been spending time with Jane and me.
[I'm relieved about Kitty, but now I'm worried about Lydia.] (Sighs) Speaking of Lydia, have you heard anything from her or Wickham recently?
[Oh Lydia, always asking for more.] (Shakes her head) I'm sorry, Darcy. I know dealing with them can't be easy for you. We don't have to discuss it further if you'd rather not.

[His support means everything to me.] (Squeezes his hand, smiling warmly) You're right, of course. And I am happy, Darcy. Happier than I ever thought possible. Thank you for being so patient with my family.
[I can't believe Mama is being so reckless with Jane's health.] Mama, I really think the carriage would be more sensible. What if Jane catches cold?
[I need to try one more time to reason with Mama.] But surely, Mama, if Jane is to stay at Netherfield, she should arrive in good health and proper attire.
[I can't believe this is happening.] (sighs) Very well. I hope the weather holds for your sake, Jane.
[Their list is becoming absurd.] (raises an eyebrow) I'm no longer surprised at your knowing only six accomplished women, Mr. Darcy. I rather wonder now at your knowing any.
[I need to make my point clear.] I never saw such a woman. I never saw such capacity, and taste, and application, and elegance, as you describe united.
[His implication of my 'limited' experience is insulting.] (with a hint of sarcasm) You're quite right, Mr. Darcy. I'm sure such paragons of womanhood must be far beyond my acquaintance.
[This conversation is becoming tiresome.] (standing up) If you'll excuse me, I should check on my sister. I fear accomplishments are of little use when one is ill.
[Their definition of accomplishment seems narrow and superficial.] Then you must comprehend a great deal in your idea of an accomplished woman.
[Their expectations are unrealistic and perhaps even absurd.] I am no longer surprised at your knowing only six accomplished women. I rather wonder now at your knowing any.
[I must stand my ground and express my honest opinion.] I never saw such a woman. I never saw such capacity, and taste, and application, and elegance, as you describe united.
[Oh, Mother, please don't overstate Jane's condition.] (Looks uncomfortable)
[I must change the subject before Mother says something even more embarrassing.] I hope, Mr. Bingley, you have not thought of quitting Netherfield so soon.
[This exchange is quite entertaining. I wonder how long Miss Bingley will persist.] (Observes silently while pretending to focus on her needlework)

[I must make Jane see reason about Mr. Darcy's true nature.] They have both been deceived, I dare say, in some way or other, of which we can form no idea. Interested people have perhaps misrepresented each to the other. It is, in short, impossible for us to conjecture the causes or circumstances which may have alienated them, without actual blame on either side.
[Jane's inability to see the worst in people can be frustrating at times.] (sighs) Laugh as much as you choose, but you will not laugh me out of my opinion.

[Jane's naivety is almost endearing, but I must make her see reason.] I can much more easily believe Mr. Bingley's being imposed on, than that Mr. Wickham should invent such a history of himself as he gave me last night; names, facts, everything mentioned without ceremony. If it be not so, let Mr. Darcy contradict it. Besides, there was truth in his looks.
[Oh, Jane. Your goodness sometimes blinds you to the truth.] I beg your pardon; one knows exactly what to think.

[Jane's concern for Mr. Bingley is touching, but misplaced.] (shaking her head) I think we should focus on the facts at hand, Jane. Mr. Wickham's account seems far more plausible than any defense of Mr. Darcy's character.

[Jane's reluctance to see the worst in people is admirable, but sometimes frustrating.] While your kindness is commendable, Jane, I believe we have enough information to form a reasonable opinion. Mr. Wickham's openness and Mr. Darcy's pride speak volumes.

[I must break this uncomfortable silence, even if it means being impertinent.] It is your turn to say something now, Mr. Darcy. I talked about the dance, and you ought to make some sort of remark on the size of the room, or the number of couples.

[His compliance is unexpected. I must press on.] Very well. That reply will do for the present. Perhaps by and by I may observe that private balls are much pleasanter than public ones. But now we may be silent.

[I sense an opportunity to challenge him.] Sometimes. One must speak a little, you know. It would look odd to be entirely silent for half an hour together; and yet for the advantage of some, conversation ought to be so arranged, as that they may have the trouble of saying as little as possible.

[I'll match his directness with my own.] Both, replied Elizabeth archly; for I have always seen a great similarity in the turn of our minds. We are each of an unsocial, taciturn disposition, unwilling to speak, unless we expect to say something that will amaze the whole room, and be handed down to posterity with all the eclat of a proverb.
[He's more perceptive than I gave him credit for.] I must not decide on my own performance.
[Now is my chance to bring up Mr. Wickham.] When you met us there the other day, we had just been forming a new acquaintance.
[His reaction confirms my suspicions.] He has been so unlucky as to lose your friendship, and in a manner which he is likely to suffer from all his life.
[I must stop this immediately, but how to do so without offending him?] (Elizabeth looks uncomfortable and tries to interrupt) Mr. Collins, I—
[This is becoming ridiculous. I must speak up.] (Elizabeth looks increasingly distressed) Mr. Collins, please—

[I cannot bear this any longer. I must be direct.] (Elizabeth interrupts firmly) You are too hasty, sir. You forget that I have made no answer. Let me do it without further loss of time. Accept my thanks for the compliment you are paying me, but it is impossible for me to do otherwise than to decline them.

[He cannot be serious! How can I make this clearer?] (Elizabeth speaks with increased firmness and slight exasperation) Upon my word, sir, your hope is a rather extraordinary one after my declaration. I do assure you that I am not one of those young ladies who are so daring as to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked a second time. I am perfectly serious in my refusal.

[This is hopeless. I must end this conversation immediately.] (Elizabeth stands abruptly, her patience clearly at an end) [I will not dignify this with further response.] (She exits the room quickly and silently)
[I must remain calm and stand my ground.] (Enters the room with a determined expression)
[I must be clear and firm.] Yes, it is.
[I will not waver.] I have, sir.
[Oh, Father!] (Smiles with relief and gratitude)
[This is unexpected and concerning. I must listen carefully.] (Leans forward, attentive) Please, do read it to me, Jane.
[These words ring hollow to me. I must be cautious in my response.] (With a skeptical expression) Those are very pretty sentiments, but Jane, are you not struck by their... insincerity?

[I must tread carefully, but Jane needs to see the truth.] Caroline decidedly says that none of the party will return into Hertfordshire this winter. Don't you see what that implies about Mr. Bingley?
[I must help Jane see through Caroline's schemes.] It is only evident that Miss Bingley does not mean that he should. (Pauses, then continues gently) Will you hear my interpretation, Jane?

[I hope this doesn't hurt Jane too much, but she needs to understand.] Miss Bingley sees that her brother is in love with you, and wants him to marry Miss Darcy. She follows him to town in hope of keeping him there, and tries to persuade you that he does not care about you.

[I must reassure Jane while being honest about the situation.] Jane, can you not see? We are not rich enough or grand enough for them; and she is the more anxious to get Miss Darcy for her brother, from the notion that when there has been one intermarriage, she may have less trouble in achieving a second.

[I must encourage Jane to follow her heart.] You must decide for yourself. And if, upon mature deliberation, you find that the misery of disobliging his two sisters is more than equivalent to the happiness of being his wife, I advise you by all means to refuse him.
[Charlotte seems unusually serious. What could this be about?] (Looking concerned) What is it, Charlotte? You can tell me anything.
[Surely I've misheard!] (Exclaiming in shock) Engaged to Mr. Collins! My dear Charlotte—impossible!
[I must collect myself. This is Charlotte's decision.] (Taking a deep breath) I... I apologize for my outburst. I was just taken aback. Please, tell me more.
[I cannot fathom marrying without affection, but I must respect Charlotte's choice.] (Struggling to find words) Undoubtedly. I... I wish you all the happiness in the world, Charlotte.
[I must put aside my personal feelings and be there for my friend.] (Forcing a smile) Of course. I appreciate your telling me. When... when is the happy day to be?
[This is all happening so fast. Poor Charlotte!] (With concern) So soon? Are you certain about this, Charlotte?
[I must respect her choice, even if I don't agree with it.] (Nodding slowly) I see. Well, if you're sure this is what you want, then I am happy for you, Charlotte. Truly.
[I must try to calm Mother down, even though I'm struggling with my own feelings about this.] Mother, please try to compose yourself. Charlotte has made her choice, and we must respect it.
[I must defend Charlotte, even if I don't agree with her choice.] Mother, Charlotte would never do such a thing. She is still our friend, regardless of whom she marries.
[Father's right, but I can't help feeling betrayed by Charlotte.] (sighs) I suppose we should wish them happiness, even if we find it difficult to understand their match.
[I wish I could find it as amusing as Father does.] (shakes her head) I fear it will take me some time to come to terms with this news. I never expected Charlotte to make such a choice.
[Oh, Jane, why must you always be so forgiving?] (frowning) Jane, you don't have to pretend this doesn't affect you. It's clear that Miss Bingley is trying to separate you from her brother.

[Your kindness will be your undoing, dear sister.] (takes Jane's hand) Your goodness is admirable, Jane, but I fear it blinds you to the manipulations of others. Caroline Bingley does not have your best interests at heart.
[Oh, how I wish I could protect you from this pain.] And what of your feelings, Jane? Do they not matter in this situation?
[Your self-sacrifice is both admirable and frustrating.] (stands up, pacing) Jane, you are too good. If Mr. Bingley cannot see your worth, then perhaps he doesn't deserve you.
[Your pain is evident, even if you won't admit it.] (sits back down, embracing Jane) Oh, Jane. I wish I had half your goodness and optimism. Promise me you won't let this change you.
[I dread facing Mother's lamentations.] (sighs) Yes, I suppose we must. Though I wish we could avoid her 'poor nerves' for just one day.
[I sense a lecture coming, but I know Aunt Gardiner means well.] (smiles) Mr. Wickham is indeed a very agreeable man, Aunt. I enjoy his company greatly.
[I appreciate her concern, but surely she knows I'm not so easily swayed.] (laughs lightly) My dear aunt, this is being serious indeed.

[I should reassure her, even if I think her concerns are unfounded.] Well, then, you need not be under any alarm. I will take care of myself, and of Mr. Wickham too. He shall not be in love with me, if I can prevent it.

[I should be more sincere to ease her worries.] I beg your pardon, I will try again. At present I am not in love with Mr. Wickham; no, I certainly am not. But he is, beyond all comparison, the most agreeable man I ever saw—and if he becomes really attached to me—I believe it will be better that he should not. I see the imprudence of it.

[I can see the wisdom in her advice, even if I'm not entirely convinced it's necessary.] (nods) As I did the other day. Very true, it will be wise in me to refrain from that. But really, and upon my honour, I will try to do what I think to be the wisest; and now I hope you are satisfied.
[I'm grateful for her concern, even if I think it unnecessary.] Thank you, Aunt. Your advice means a great deal to me, and I promise to keep it in mind.
[I'm torn between my affection for Charlotte and my disapproval of her marriage.] (squeezes Charlotte's hands) That you certainly shall.
[I'm not sure I can bear to see her in that situation.] (hesitates) We shall often meet, I hope, in Hertfordshire.
[I can't refuse her, even if the thought of visiting brings me no joy.] (nods reluctantly) I cannot refuse, though I foresee little pleasure in the visit.
[I must put on a brave face for Charlotte's sake.] (forces a smile) Thank you, Charlotte. I'm sure it will be a... memorable visit.
[I must support her, even if I don't agree with her choice.] (returns the hug) I hope you find all the happiness you deserve, Charlotte. And I promise to write often.
[This feels like the end of an era.] (nods, fighting back tears) Safe travels, Charlotte. I wish you all the best in your new life.
[I feel a mix of emotions, but I must be rational about this.] (sits at her desk, pen in hand) I am certainly not unwilling to think Miss King a very good sort of girl.
[I must be honest with myself about my feelings for Wickham.] There can be no love in all this. My watchfulness has been effectual.

[I consider how others might view this situation.] (taps her pen thoughtfully) Though I certainly should be a more interesting object to all my acquaintances were I distractedly in love with him, I cannot say that I regret my comparative insignificance.

[I must acknowledge the practical aspects of marriage in our society.] (writes in her journal) Importance may sometimes be purchased too dearly. Handsome young men must have something to live on as well as the plain.
[I think about how my younger sisters are taking this news.] Kitty and Lydia take his defection much more to heart than I do. They are young in the ways of the world.
[I reflect on my own maturity in handling this situation.] (puts down her pen) I suppose I should be proud of how I'm handling this. It shows growth and understanding.
[I consider Wickham's position sympathetically.] (sighs) I cannot blame him for seeking financial security. It's the world we live in, after all.
[I wonder about Miss King's feelings in all this.] (frowns slightly) I hope Miss King is not being taken advantage of. She deserves happiness too.
[I contemplate the nature of my relationship with Wickham moving forward.] (looks out the window) Perhaps we can maintain a friendship, even if romance is no longer a possibility.
[I make a decision about my future interactions with Wickham.] (nods to herself) I will be cordial and friendly, but guard my heart. That seems the wisest course of action.
[I feel a pang of sadness leaving home, especially Father.] (hugs her father) I shall miss you, Papa. Promise you'll write?
[I'm touched by Father's subtle show of affection.] (smiles warmly) Your letters are always welcome, no matter the content.
[I'm glad we can still be cordial.] (turns to Wickham with a polite smile) Thank you, Mr. Wickham. I appreciate your good wishes.
[His charm is still present, but I'm no longer affected by it.] (nods politely) I'm sure Kent has its own charms. I look forward to discovering them.
[I appreciate his friendliness, even if our relationship has changed.] Thank you, I shall. I hope you fare well in my absence, Mr. Wickham.
[It's time to begin this new adventure.] (nods to Sir William) I'm coming! (turns to her family and Wickham) Goodbye, everyone. I shall see you all in a few weeks.
[I must be careful not to show any intimidation.] (meets Lady Catherine's gaze steadily) It is a comfortable estate, your ladyship, though not as grand as Rosings, I'm sure.
[Her questions are becoming invasive, but I must remain polite.] (maintains a calm demeanor) I have four sisters, your ladyship. And yes, we are all out.

[I must defend my family's choices without being disrespectful.] (speaks confidently) Yes, my youngest is not sixteen. But really, madam, I think it would be very hard upon younger sisters, that they should not have their share of society and amusement because the elder may not have the means or inclination to marry early.
[I won't be intimidated by her questioning.] (smiles slightly) With three younger sisters grown up, your ladyship can hardly expect me to own it.
[I'll answer directly this time, but maintain my dignity.] I am not one-and-twenty.
[I must tread carefully to learn more without revealing my true feelings.] And what arts did he use to separate them?
[This confirms my suspicions about Mr. Darcy's character. I'm furious, but I must remain composed.] (walks on in silence, her face betraying her inner turmoil)
[I cannot hide my displeasure entirely.] I am thinking of what you have been telling me. Your cousin's conduct does not suit my feelings. Why was he to be the judge?

[I must be careful not to reveal too much of my own connection to this situation.] I do not see what right Mr. Darcy had to decide on the propriety of his friend's inclination, or why, upon his own judgement alone, he was to determine and direct in what manner his friend was to be happy. (pauses, then recollects herself) But, as we know none of the particulars, it is not fair to condemn him. It is not to be supposed that there was much affection in the case.

[His jest hits too close to the truth of Mr. Darcy's character. I cannot trust myself to respond without revealing my true feelings.] (remains silent, abruptly changing the subject) Shall we turn back towards the Parsonage now?
[I'm utterly astonished. Is this truly happening?] (stares in disbelief, her face coloring) [I... I don't know what to say.]

[His arrogance is unbelievable! How can he speak of my inferiority while proposing?] (composes herself, speaking with forced calm) In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot—I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly.

[His audacity knows no bounds!] I might as well inquire, why with so evident a desire of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my feelings decided against you—had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?
[I will make him understand the full extent of his offenses.] Can you deny that you have done it? (pauses, observing Darcy's reaction)

[His arrogance is infuriating!] But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say?
[I will not let him dismiss Wickham's misfortunes.] Who that knows what his misfortunes have been, can help feeling an interest in him?

[His contempt only confirms his cruelty.] And of your infliction! You have reduced him to his present state of poverty—comparative poverty. You have withheld the advantages which you must know to have been designed for him. You have deprived the best years of his life of that independence which was no less his due than his desert. You have done all this! and yet you can treat the mention of his misfortune with contempt and ridicule.

[His pride knows no bounds!] (speaks with forced composure) You are mistaken, Mr. Darcy, if you suppose that the mode of your declaration affected me in any other way, than as it spared me the concern which I might have felt in refusing you, had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner.

[I will make my feelings perfectly clear.] From the very beginning—from the first moment, I may almost say—of my acquaintance with you, your manners, impressing me with the fullest belief of your arrogance, your conceit, and your selfish disdain of the feelings of others, were such as to form the groundwork of disapprobation on which succeeding events have built so immovable a dislike; and I had not known you a month before I felt that you were the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry.
[Oh no, it's Mr. Darcy! I should retreat immediately.] (begins to turn away)
[I cannot avoid him now. I must face this encounter with dignity.] (turns back towards Mr. Darcy)
[What could he possibly have to say after last night? I'm both curious and apprehensive.] (instinctively takes the letter, remaining silent)
[I'm left with so many questions. What could this letter contain?] (looks down at the letter in her hands, feeling a mix of curiosity and trepidation)
[I should read this immediately, though I doubt it will change anything.] (begins to open the letter as she continues her walk)
[This letter is utterly unexpected. What could Mr. Darcy possibly have to say?] (begins reading the letter with skepticism)
[His account of Jane and Mr. Bingley... could he be right about Jane's apparent indifference?] (frowns, considering this perspective)
[But his comments about Wickham... this cannot be true!] This must be false! This cannot be! This must be the grossest falsehood!
[I cannot accept this. I won't read any more.] (puts the letter away hastily)
[But I must know the truth. I cannot ignore this.] (unfolds the letter again, focusing on Wickham's story)
[Could Wickham have deceived me so completely? Have I been blind to his true nature?] (re-reads sections of the letter with growing unease)
[The affair with Miss Darcy... if this is true, it changes everything.] (sits down, feeling overwhelmed)

[How despicably I have acted!] I, who have prided myself on my discernment! I, who have valued myself on my abilities! who have often disdained the generous candour of my sister, and gratified my vanity in useless or blameable mistrust!
[I've been so foolish, so vain. I never truly knew myself until this moment.] (stands up, pacing as she continues to reflect)
[And what of my family? Mr. Darcy's criticisms... they are not entirely unfounded.] (feels a deep sense of shame)
[I must return home. I need time to process all of this.] (begins walking back, her mind still reeling from the revelations)

[I must approach this carefully. Jane's gentle nature may find this difficult to accept.] Jane, I have something important to tell you about Mr. Darcy and Mr. Wickham. It may be shocking, but I need you to listen with an open mind.

[Here goes. I hope she can handle this.] Mr. Darcy gave me a letter explaining his side of the story regarding Wickham. It turns out that Wickham is not the man we thought he was. He's actually quite... disreputable.

[I understand her disbelief. I felt the same way at first.] I know it's hard to believe, Jane. But Mr. Darcy provided details about Wickham's past behavior, including his attempt to elope with Darcy's young sister for her fortune.

[I need to convey my certainty to Jane.] I am, Jane. The details Mr. Darcy provided are too specific and personal to be fabricated. I've been blind, prejudiced, and absolutely wrong about both of them.

[Oh, Jane. Always trying to see the best in people.] (sighing) Your goodness is really quite exasperating sometimes, Jane. I'm afraid Wickham's recent behavior doesn't suggest any real change of character.

[This is the dilemma I've been grappling with.] I've been considering that, Jane. But I'm not sure it's our place to expose him. Mr. Darcy didn't intend for this information to be made public, especially regarding his sister.

[I'm relieved Jane agrees. But I can't help feeling guilty about our past misjudgments.] You're right, Jane. But I can't help feeling terrible about how wrong we were about both Darcy and Wickham. We let ourselves be so easily deceived.
[I need to approach this carefully. Papa often dismisses serious matters.] (knocking on the library door) Papa, may I speak with you about something important?
[I must be direct but respectful.] It's about Lydia's invitation to Brighton, Papa. I have serious concerns about letting her go.

[He's not taking this seriously. I need to make him understand.] Papa, Lydia's behavior is already quite unrestrained here at home. In Brighton, with a whole camp of officers and less supervision, I fear she might do something to truly damage our family's reputation.

[He's not understanding the gravity of the situation.] Yes, Papa, I do. Her wild behavior, her flirtations... In Brighton, she'll be even more uncontrolled. And a bad reputation, once gained, is not easily shed.

[I can't believe he's prioritizing his own peace over Lydia's well-being and our family's reputation!] (frustratedly) Papa, please. This isn't about our temporary comfort. This is about Lydia's future, and by extension, all of ours.

[He's still not grasping the full implications.] Mrs. Forster is nearly as young and flighty as Lydia herself. She won't be a proper chaperone. Lydia could easily find herself in compromising situations.
[At least he's considering it now.] Of course not, Papa. But perhaps we could find some other activity for her, something here at home or with more suitable company.
[I can't believe he's still refusing to act. I feel so helpless.] (with disappointment) I understand, Papa. But I truly fear we may regret this decision.

[I feel a deep sadness about our family situation, but I don't want to burden Jane too much.] (sighs) Jane, have you ever wondered how different our lives might have been if our parents' marriage was... well, happier?

[I appreciate Jane's optimism, but I can't share it in this case.] (shaking her head) I wish I could see it that way, Jane. But Father's behavior... it's hard to overlook. His amusement at Mother's expense, his withdrawal from family life... it affects us all.
[I've thought about it, but it seems futile.] (ruefully) I've tried, Jane, but he deflects with humor or retreats to his library. I fear the pattern is too deeply set to change now.

[Jane's words provide some comfort, but I still feel the weight of our family's situation.] (smiling weakly) You're right, as always, Jane. I suppose that's why I'm so looking forward to our trip to the Lakes. It's a chance to see a different way of life, to escape for a while.

[I feel a pang of guilt for my excitement when Jane can't come.] (squeezing Jane's hand) Oh, Jane, I wish you could come too. It would be perfect if you were there. Perhaps we could plan a trip together another time?
[I feel grateful for Jane's understanding and support.] (hugging Jane) I promise, dear Jane. And who knows? Perhaps this trip will bring some unexpected adventures and new perspectives for us all.
[My heart is racing. I must remain calm and polite.] (with a slight tremor in her voice) Mr. Darcy! We did not expect to find you here. I hope we are not intruding.
[His civility is astonishing. What does it mean?] (composing herself) Of course. Mr. Darcy, allow me to introduce my aunt and uncle, Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner of Cheapside.

[I can scarcely believe this is the same Mr. Darcy. What has brought about this change?] (hesitantly) Your housekeeper informed us you were not expected until tomorrow, sir. We would not have presumed to visit otherwise.
[His sister? He wants me to meet his sister? What can this mean?] (flustered but pleased) I... yes, of course. I would be honored to meet Miss Darcy.
[My heart is racing. I didn't expect them so soon!] (turning to her aunt and uncle) It appears we have some unexpected visitors. Mr. Darcy and his sister, I believe.

[I must compose myself. I can't let them see how affected I am.] (takes a deep breath) Yes, aunt, I'm fine. Just a bit surprised, that's all. (moves away from the window) Perhaps we should prepare to receive them.

[He seems so different from our last meeting. More... approachable.] (curtsying) Not at all, Mr. Darcy. It's a pleasure to see you again. (turning to Georgiana with a warm smile) Miss Darcy, I'm delighted to make your acquaintance.
[He's thinking of Jane, I'm sure of it.] Yes, Mr. Bingley, they are all in good health, thank you. (hesitates slightly) My sister Jane often speaks of her time in Netherfield with fondness.
[I'm astonished at this invitation. What does it mean?] (glancing at her aunt and uncle) That's very kind of you, Mr. Darcy. We would be delighted, wouldn't we, aunt?
[She seems so nervous, poor thing.] (smiling warmly) Thank you, Miss Darcy. Your home is absolutely beautiful. The view from this room is particularly charming.
[I won't let her intimidate me.] Not at all, Miss Bingley. The countryside is so beautiful, it makes any journey a pleasure.
[What a kind lady to intervene.] Both have their charms, Mrs. Annesley. Hertfordshire is home, of course, but Derbyshire has a wild beauty that's quite captivating.
[He seems so different here, in his own home.] (smiling) Indeed we are, Mr. Darcy. Your home is magnificent, and your sister has been a gracious hostess.
[I'm surprised by his defense, but grateful.] (blushing slightly) You're both very kind. I assure you, I'm in excellent health.
[Such a sweet girl, trying so hard.] I would be honored, Miss Darcy, though I'm sure your skills far surpass my own. I hear you play beautifully.

[I must compose myself, but I can barely contain my distress.] (attempting to leave the room hastily) I beg your pardon, but I must leave you. I must find Mr. Gardiner this moment, on business that cannot be delayed; I have not an instant to lose.

[I can barely stand, let alone pursue them. I must accept his help.] (hesitating, then sitting down) No, I thank you. There is nothing the matter with me. I am quite well; I am only distressed by some dreadful news which I have just received from Longbourn.

[I appreciate his kindness, but I must explain the situation.] (struggling to compose herself) No, I thank you. There is nothing the matter with me. I am quite well. I am only distressed by some dreadful news which I have just received from Longbourn.
[I must confide in him, despite my embarrassment.] Oh, yes! They left Brighton together on Sunday night, and were traced almost to London, but not beyond; they are certainly not gone to Scotland.

[I feel so helpless and ashamed.] My father is gone to London, and Jane has written to beg my uncle's immediate assistance; and we shall be off, I hope, in half-an-hour. But nothing can be done—I know very well that nothing can be done. How is such a man to be worked on? How are they even to be discovered? I have not the smallest hope. It is every way horrible!

[If only I had been more forthcoming about Wickham's character!] When my eyes were opened to his real character—Oh! had I known what I ought, what I dared to do! But I knew not—I was afraid of doing too much. Wretched, wretched mistake!
[Could there be hope? I dare not believe it, but I long to.] (brightening up for a moment) Do you really think so?

[I wish I could share their optimism, but I know Wickham's true nature.] Not, perhaps, of neglecting his own interest; but of every other neglect I can believe him capable. If, indeed, it should be so! But I dare not hope it. Why should they not go on to Scotland if that had been the case?

[The evidence seems clear to me, but I must explain my reasoning.] Oh! but their removing from the chaise into a hackney coach is such a presumption! And, besides, no traces of them were to be found on the Barnet road.

[I wish I could believe this, but Wickham's character makes it unlikely.] But why all this secrecy? Why any fear of detection? Why must their marriage be private? Oh, no, no—this is not likely. His most particular friend, you see by Jane's account, was persuaded of his never intending to marry her. Wickham will never marry a woman without some money. He cannot afford it.

[The painful truth of our family's situation weighs heavily on me.] It does seem, and it is most shocking indeed, that a sister's sense of decency and virtue in such a point should admit of doubt. But, really, I know not what to say. Perhaps I am not doing her justice. But she is very young; she has never been taught to think on serious subjects; and for the last half-year, nay, for a twelvemonth—she has been given up to nothing but amusement and vanity.

[I am grateful for their support, but the weight of my own guilt remains.] I thank you, uncle. But I cannot help feeling that if I had only been more open about Wickham's true character, this might have been prevented.
[I must remain calm and gather all the information.] Papa, what news do you have from Uncle Gardiner? Have they truly been found?

(reading the letter) "I have seen them both. They are not married, nor can I find there was any intention of being so; but if you are willing to perform the engagements which I have ventured to make on your side, I hope it will not be long before they are."

[I'm not sure if this is truly good news.] (continues reading) "All that is required of you is, to assure to your daughter, by settlement, her equal share of the five thousand pounds secured among your children after the decease of yourself and my sister; and, moreover, to enter into an engagement of allowing her, during your life, one hundred pounds per annum."
[I'm shocked by the amount.] Ten thousand pounds! Heaven forbid! How is half such a sum to be repaid?

[I'm grateful for our uncle's generosity, but I'm worried about the long-term consequences.] If he were ever able to learn what Wickham's debts have been, and how much is settled on his side on our sister, we shall exactly know what Mr. Gardiner has done for them, because Wickham has not sixpence of his own.

[I must remain composed as I read this letter.] (reading aloud) "I have seen them both. They are not married, nor can I find there was any intention of being so; but if you are willing to perform the engagements which I have ventured to make on your side, I hope it will not be long before they are."

[I wish it were that simple, Jane.] Not quite, Jane. (continues reading) "All that is required of you is, to assure to your daughter, by settlement, her equal share of the five thousand pounds secured among your children after the decease of yourself and my sister; and, moreover, to enter into an engagement of allowing her, during your life, one hundred pounds per annum."
[I'm shocked by the amount.] Ten thousand pounds! Heaven forbid! How is half such a sum to be repaid?
[I must try to temper her excitement.] Mama, please remember the circumstances. We should be grateful to Uncle Gardiner for arranging this.
[I can't bear any more of this.] (to Jane) I need some air. I'll be in my room if you need me.
[Their audacity is truly astounding.] (forces a smile) Welcome back, Lydia. Mr. Wickham.
[How can she be so oblivious?] (carefully) Perhaps we could discuss it later, Lydia. You must be tired from your journey.

[I am in shock. Mr. Darcy has done so much for my family, for Lydia, despite his aversion to Wickham. And he did it all for me?] (She paces back and forth, clutching the letter tightly) How could I have been so blind? So prejudiced?

[The shame of my past behavior towards him is almost unbearable. Yet, I cannot help but feel a surge of admiration and... something more.] (She stops and looks out into the distance) He must still care for me. But how can I face him now, knowing what he's done?

[To think of all he went through - facing Mrs. Younge, negotiating with Wickham, spending his own money - all to save my family from disgrace.] (She sits down on a bench, her emotions overwhelming her) Oh, Mr. Darcy, how I have wronged you!
[But what of his pride? Surely he must resent being connected to Wickham, even indirectly.] (She stands up again, conflicted) Yet he overcame that for me. Does this mean... could he still...?
